summary: Ecclesiastes 3 (22 verses) continues the story of vanity. Starting with 'For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:', it moves through themes of vanity, time and calls readers toward fear God.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows vanity lived out in jerusalem reflections. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice, and to do good as long as they live.
Therefore I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works, for that is his portion; for who can bring him to see what will be after him?

questions.question: What is happening in Ecclesiastes 3?
questions.answer: In 22 verses, this chapter ecclesiastes 3 (22 verses) continues the story of vanity. starting with 'for everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:', it moves through themes of vanity, time and calls readers toward fear god. The setting is jerusalem reflections, written to seekers. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ecclesiastes and why 3 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally qoheleth, solomon tradition, addressed to seekers around ~900 bc debate. This chapter fits the book's purpose as philosophical wisdom — its themes of vanity, time build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'righteousness' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Being in right standing, doing what is right. In this chapter, it appears in context of vanity. For a first-time reader: think of it as being in right standing, doing what is right, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through vanity and time, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 19 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'For that which happens to the sons of men happens to animals. Even one thing happens to them. As the one dies, so the other dies. Yes, they have all one breath; and man has no adva...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about vanity. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?

glossary.def: Being in right standing, doing what is right
